title: Audit log archival, indexing, and backfill implementation notes
summary: Implementation notes for audit log storage and retention: design choices for hot/cold/archive tiers, indexing strategies to support SIEM exports and fast forensic queries, backfill and reindex approaches that are idempotent and resumable, legal-hold handling, and common failure modes with mitigations.
content:
Purpose
This working doc captures engineering decisions and runbook-level implementation notes for the audit logging pipeline: storage tiers, retention windows, indexing strategies, backfill processes, and failure modes. Target audience: eng (platform, infra), security, compliance, and SRE who will operate and extend the system.

Goals and constraints
- Preserve tamper-evident audit trail for required retention windows (see retention matrix below).
- Provide sub-second search for recent (hot) data for investigations and SIEM forwarding; queryable day-range for cold tier via index.
- Minimize storage costs by using tiered lifecycle policies and compressed format while keeping ability to rehydrate for forensic queries/backfills.
- Backfills must be idempotent, checkpointed, and resumable across restarts.
- Support legal holds (freeze TTL) per-tenant or per-evidence-id with strong authorization checks.

Retention and tiering matrix (policy)
- Hot tier (primary index): 0-90 days, SSD-backed, real-time indexing, retained for fast search and alerts.
- Warm tier (query-optimized blobs + secondary index): 91-365 days, compressed columnar store plus light index for range queries.
- Cold/archive tier: 1-7 years (customer + regulatory), object storage (S3/GS), encrypted, index-minimal (time-range metadata). Must support rehydration for ad-hoc reindex.
- Legal hold: indefinite until release; marks entries in metadata store and prevents TTL deletion.

Data lifecycle implementation notes
- Ingest path writes to primary append-only Kafka topic partitioned by tenant_id (primary key) and day. Messages include sequence_number, event_ts, tenant_id, event_type, payload_checksum, schema_version, and encryption_metadata.
- Primary consumer pipeline does lightweight validation and writes two artifacts in a single atomic operation per message: (1) write to hot storage (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch index) and (2) write raw protobuf/ndjson to object store under /raw/YYYY/MM/DD/tenant/. Object-level dedupe uses message checksum.
- A daily compaction job consolidates per-tenant raw files into day-sharded compressed blobs and emits metadata events for warm-tier indexing.

Indexing strategy
- Hot index: optimized for TTL, term queries on tenant_id, event_type, actor_id, and recent time ranges. Use time-based indices (daily) with ILM to roll into warm. Map schema to limit fields in hot to essential search fields (no large payloads).
- Warm index: secondary inverted index built from compressed day-sharded blobs. Contains a superset of searchable fields but excludes heavy free-text. Warm index built by a scheduled reindex job that reads compacted blobs and writes into a purpose-built warm index store (could be OpenSearch optimized for denser storage or a columnar DB with secondary lookup).
- Metadata index: small dedicated index for legal-hold flags, retention deadlines, and backfill checkpoints. This index is the single source of truth for deletion eligibility.

Backfill and reindexing design
- Backfill use-cases: (1) rebuild warm index after schema change; (2) reimport historical data to recover missed days; (3) rehydrate cold data for forensic queries; (4) export to SIEM for historical window.
- Principles: idempotence, checkpointing, parallelism by tenant-day shard, and bounded resource usage.
- Job model: backfill jobs are short-lived workers that claim work units from the metadata queue (work unit = tenant_id + day). Workers run: fetch raw compacted blob -> validate checksum -> transform (schema migration) -> upsert into target index using deterministic doc_id = sha256(tenant_id + event_ts + seq_no).
- Checkpointing: each worker periodically commits highest-processed sequence_number for current work unit into metadata index. On restart, worker resumes from checkpoint.
- Concurrency: a distributed lock per work unit prevents duplicate work. Workers use optimistic concurrency when upserting into index to avoid duplicates and preserve ordering where necessary.

Failure modes and mitigations
- Data loss on concurrent writes: ensure append-only Kafka topic and write-through to object store with synchronous ack. Use message checksum and compacted topic retention for 7 days to allow replay.
- Partial backfill failures (OOM, crash): worker should persist progress to metadata index every N events (configurable, default 5000). On failure, supervisor requeues remainder. Alerting: backfill-worker-failure per-tenant-day.
- Index mapping change causing rejection: use blue/green reindex strategy—create new index with new mapping, backfill into new index, then atomically switch alias. Keep old index until retention deadline.
- Cold rehydration latency spikes: rehydration jobs should be throttled via token bucket (global) and per-tenant quotas. Use pre-warming option for legal requests (SLA 6 hours) that prioritizes small subsets.
- SIEM export lag or duplication: exporter must maintain export_checkpoint per destination (Splunk indexer or ES endpoint). Implement exactly-once semantics using idempotent keys for exported events and dedupe at destination when possible.

Operational instrumentation and alerts
- Metrics to emit: ingestion_lag_ms (per-tenant), hot_index_write_errors, compaction_failure_rate, backfill_success_rate, rehydration_latency_p50/p95/p99, legal_hold_count, deletion_jobs_blocked.
- Alerts: ingestion_lag > 5m for >5 tenants -> P1; backfill_worker_errors rate > 5% over 1h -> P2; compaction failure for 3 consecutive runs -> P2; rehydration SLA miss -> P1.
- Dashboards: hot/warm index size, daily shard counts, per-tenant retention consumption, expected next-deletion cutover list.

Legal hold and compliance hooks
- Legal hold API: writes a hold record (tenant_id, evidence_id(s), hold_reason, issued_by, issued_ts) to metadata index. Deletion worker checks hold records and skips deletion for held evidence.
- Hold release requires multi-person approval recorded in metadata. All hold actions are themselves audit-logged to immutable append store.

Cost and storage sizing notes (rough estimates)
- For 100TB/year raw ingestion: hot tier (0-90d) ~10% of total; warm tier ~20%; cold/archive ~70%. Compression and dedupe are expected to reduce storage by 3–4x in cold tier.
- Estimate lifecycle costs and include rehydration cost in budget planning; occasional large forensic rehydrates can spike egress and read IOPS.

Runbook: common procedures
- Recover a failed backfill job:
  1) Check metadata index for checkpoint for tenant-day.
  2) Inspect worker logs and last successful seq_no.
  3) If transient error, restart worker; if OOM, scale worker resources and restart.
  4) If data corruption (checksum mismatch), mark work unit as needs-manual-review and alert infra + security.

- Emergency rehydrate for compliance/legal request:
  1) Create rehydrate_ticket in ticketing system and attach legal_hold if required.
  2) Kick off targeted rehydration job for tenant + date-range; set high priority and per-tenant throttle adjustment.
  3) Monitor rehydration job metrics and confirm exported data integrity via checksum comparison.

Open design questions / TODOs
- Decide warm-index backend: OpenSearch with aggressive ILM or a columnar store (Dremel-style) for cheaper, faster analytical queries.
- Define exact SLA for legal rehydration (default 24h vs expedited 6h).
- Finalize export format for SIEM (CEF vs JSON ECS) and implement field-mapping table.
- Build a test harness for backfills that simulates duplicate messages, out-of-order events, and partial writes.

Appendix: example work-unit checkpoint document (metadata index)
{
  "work_unit": "tenant123::2025-11-02",
  "status": "in_progress",
  "last_seq_no": "3456789",
  "worker_id": "backfill-7f29",
  "started_at": "2026-02-20T18:12:02Z"
}

Notes and references
- See linked artifacts above for schema and related runbooks. Keep this doc as the lightweight implementation guide; migrate stable policies to the official compliance playbook once design decisions are finalized.
